label: Unit 2
theme: Tell the Doctor What You Feel
intro: He has the part names. Now let him use them in a pretend visit: where it hurts, what it feels like, and when it started. Give him time to finish before you supply the missing bit.

gelds.text: A complete report of where, what and when
Asking what a doctor tool does
Heart and lungs recalled during a visit
Visit and handwashing steps in order

tryNote: A stuffed animal can be the patient. Use pretend symptoms; he does not need a real hurt to practise.

daily.title: Let the patient talk
daily.do: Pretend the bear bumped its foot. He tells you which part hurts. Wait for the name.
daily.stretch: He speaks for the bear in a whole sentence, adds what the hurt feels like and when it began, then tells another grown-up without your help.

daily.title: Ask before the tool
daily.do: Take turns being the doctor. He points to his chest and asks what the pretend stethoscope does before you listen.
daily.stretch: He explains how listening helps the doctor hear his heart, recalls that the heart pushes blood and lungs take in air, then puts arrival, telling, asking and listening in order.
daily.skill: Explaining a tool and sequencing a visit

daily.title: Hands before food
daily.do: Wash together: wet, soap, scrub for twenty seconds, rinse, dry. Let him supply the next step.
daily.stretch: He runs the same routine himself and says why it comes before food and after blowing his nose. Watch the fingertips; that is where the shortcut happens.

goalsTitle: What he should have by the end of this unit

his: Names the part that hurts and describes the feeling in a complete sentence.
Tells what happened first and when the discomfort began.
Points to his heart and explains that the doctor's stethoscope helps listen to it, recalling what the heart and lungs do.
Puts a pretend visit in order and asks what a tool will do before the examination.
Washes his hands independently and explains why he does it before eating and after blowing his nose.

weekend: Run a whole pretend visit with a different grown-up listening. Let him give the report, ask about the tool, and say what comes next.

songs.title: Where, What, When
songs.style: Start singing immediately, with no instrumental intro. Gentle ukulele, soft hand claps and a simple call-and-response tune. One clear warm voice, short repeated melody, steady preschool pace, clean ending without a long outro.
lyrics: Heart goes thump, lungs take air.
Ask what the tools do there.

basic.label: Hand
basic.note: Your hand can point to the part that hurts.

basic.label: Foot
basic.note: Say which foot hurts when you tell the doctor.

basic.label: Eye
basic.note: Your eyes help you see the tool before it touches you.

basic.label: Ear
basic.note: Your ears hear the doctor explain the tool.

basic.label: Nose
basic.note: A tissue catches what comes out when you blow your nose.

basic.label: Mouth
basic.note: You can open your mouth for the doctor to look inside.

advanced.label: Heart
advanced.note: Your heart pushes blood around your body.

advanced.label: Lungs
advanced.note: Your lungs take in air when you breathe.

advanced.label: Stethoscope
advanced.note: The doctor listens to sounds inside your chest with a stethoscope.

advanced.label: Thermometer
advanced.note: A thermometer measures how warm your body is.

advanced.label: Scale
advanced.note: A scale measures how much you weigh.

advanced.label: Bandage
advanced.note: A bandage covers a small scrape.

advanced.label: Soap
advanced.note: Soap helps wash dirt and germs off your hands.

advanced.label: Tissue
advanced.note: Blow your nose into a tissue, then put it in the bin.

sort.title: Where, What and When?
sort.sub: All three parts or something missing
sort.noSay: Right. One part still needs telling.
sort.retry: Listen for the part, the feeling and when it started.

items.text: You say, "My foot feels sore since I bumped it at play."
items.note: Foot says where, sore says what, and the bump tells when.

items.text: You say, "It hurts."
items.note: The listener still needs where and when.

items.text: You say, "My ear started aching this morning."
items.note: Ear, aching and this morning give all three parts.

items.text: You say, "Something feels bad."
items.note: Something does not name a part or a starting time.

items.text: You say, "My knee has stung since I fell on the path."
items.note: Knee, stung and the fall give the listener a full report.

items.text: You say, "Over there."
items.note: The listener needs the part, the feeling and when it began.

items.text: You say, "My throat started hurting at breakfast."
items.note: Throat, hurting and breakfast give all three parts.

items.text: You say, "I got hurt at play."
items.note: Play tells when, but the part and feeling are missing.

items.text: You say, "My finger has felt sore since I pinched it in the toy box."
items.note: Finger, sore and the pinch give all three parts.

items.text: You say, "My knee stings."
items.note: The part and feeling are there; when it started is missing.

items.text: You say, "After running, my ankle started aching."
items.note: The parts can come in a different order and still tell where, what and when.

items.text: You say, "It has stung since breakfast."
items.note: The feeling and time still leave out the body part.

items.text: You say, "At lunch my head began to ache."
items.note: Lunch gives when, head gives where and ache gives what.

items.text: You point to your knee and say, "It stings since I fell."
items.note: Pointing helps, but the words still need the name knee.

sort.title: Ready for Clean Hands?
sort.sub: Helps keep clean or Needs a change

items.text: You wash with soap before eating.
items.note: Soap and rinsing help clean your hands before they touch food.

items.text: You wipe muddy hands on your shirt and eat.
items.note: The shirt does not wash your hands.

items.text: You put your used tissue in the bin.
items.note: A used tissue belongs in the bin.

items.text: You leave a used tissue on the dinner table.
items.note: The table needs to stay clear of used tissues.

items.text: You wash after blowing your nose.
items.note: Your hands touched the tissue near your nose.

items.text: You rinse off all the soap.
items.note: Rinsing carries the soap and loosened dirt away.

items.text: You eat with soap still on your fingers.
items.note: Rinse the soap off before touching food.

items.text: You dry washed hands with a clean towel.
items.note: The clean towel dries your clean hands.

items.text: You rub your eyes with muddy fingers.
items.note: Wash the mud off before touching your face.

items.text: Your hands look clean after blowing your nose, so you skip washing.
items.note: You cannot see every germ on your hands.

items.text: You cough into your elbow instead of your hand.
items.note: Your hands stay out of the cough.

items.text: You wash, then pick up muddy shoes and start eating.
items.note: Touching muddy shoes means the hands need washing again.

items.text: You turn off the tap while you scrub with soap.
items.note: You can save water while you scrub, then turn it on to rinse.

items.text: You share a towel that is already covered in dirt.
items.note: Use a clean towel after washing.

steps.text: Hear how it listens to your heart
Let the doctor listen after the explanation

sets.goal: Tell the bear story in order

steps.text: Bear bumps a foot on a block
Bear says the foot feels sore
Bear says it began after the bump
The doctor shows a listening tool
